extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of aesthetics; artists, poets, designers, and critics interested in theories of beauty
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and presents criteria for what constitutes beauty (and what does not) in natural and artistic objects, distinguishing beauty from proportion, fitness, and perfection, and identifying positive sensory qualities (size, smoothness, gradual variation) that produce the passion of love. Useful for anyone evaluating or producing aesthetically pleasing work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion not the cause of Beauty in the Human Species.
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion (precise measures or ratios) is not the principal cause of beauty; beauty arises from manner rather than exact measurement. The idea of a 'common form' makes proportion considered, but it is manner (how parts are arranged/treated) that creates beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance argue that ornamental design shows manner, not exact proportions, produces beauty; architectural analogies (e.g., building proportions said to come from the human body) are forced and often irrelevant — human figures rarely assume the postures invoked, and many well-regarded buildings do not conform to the supposed 'square' derived from a man with arms extended. Practitioners should not rely on fixed numeric proportions alone when aiming for beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion further considered.
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice in favor of proportion arises from a mistaken equation of deformity with the opposite of beauty; removing causes of deformity does not necessarily produce beauty. Proportion and customary measures commonly found in mankind are often present without producing beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom and use create expectations (common form), but beauty often strikes by novelty rather than conformity. The presence of 'common proportions' often yields mediocrity rather than the passions; therefore, the mere absence of deformity (or conformity to customary proportions) is insufficient as a test for beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness not the cause of Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that beauty is the result of utility or parts being well adapted to their ends (fitness) is false: many well-fitted / useful parts are not beautiful, and many beautiful things show no obvious utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative counterexamples: a pig's snout, a pelican's pouch, hedgehogs, porcupines, elephants' trunks, and monkeys' anatomies are highly fit for their purposes yet not seen as beautiful; conversely, human legs (less optimally adapted for running than a horse's) are judged beautiful. Therefore landscapers, artists, and writers should not substitute functional fitness for aesthetic appeal when designing for beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: The real effects of Fitness.
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion and fitness have value in works of art, but their effect is intellectual approval (approbation) of the understanding rather than the passion of love elicited by beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fitness is recognized through study (e.g., understanding a watch's mechanism), it produces admiration of contrivance rather than immediate beauty; in art, fitness helps achieve appropriate ends (a hall vs a gallery) and supports good sense and experience, but ornament, surface treatment, and qualities that strike the imagination produce stronger feelings of beauty. Practically: design for purpose, but use ornament and sensory qualities to evoke passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection not the cause of Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection (as such) is not the constituent cause of beauty; in some cases high perfection in the female is associated with ideas of weakness or imperfection rather than loveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes social behaviors (affectations of weakness, modesty, blushing) that increase perceived beauty, suggesting that apparent imperfection or vulnerability can heighten loveliness. Thus, aiming for mechanical/perfect execution alone may not produce the aesthetic affection associated with beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: How far the idea of Beauty may be applied to the Qualities of the Mind.
rubrics_metrics.description: Grand, sublime virtues (fortitude, justice, wisdom) produce admiration or even terror rather than love; softer virtues (ease of temper, compassion, kindness, liberality) engage our hearts and are perceived as lovely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing character in writing or portraiture, emphasize softer, familiar virtues to evoke affection and loveliness; reserve the language of beauty carefully when describing mind/virtue to avoid conflating reverence and love.

rubrics_metrics.name: The real cause of Beauty.
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty largely consists in positive sensible qualities in bodies that act mechanically upon the human mind via the senses rather than being products of reason or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find what makes things beautiful, attend to how sensible qualities are disposed in objects that historically and experientially produce love or corresponding affection. This directs attention to sensory/formal properties (size, surface, line, variation) rather than abstract principles like proportion, fitness, or perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful objects small.
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent/quantity matters: objects of love (the beautiful) are typically comparatively small; languages tend to use diminutives for objects of affection. By contrast, the sublime and admiration dwell on large, terrible, or great objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evoking tenderness or loveliness (e.g., in characters, creatures, details), favor smaller scale and diminutive qualities; to provoke admiration or the sublime, use grand or large-scale forms. This is a tool for tonal control in creative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness.
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoothness is a consistently observable and essential property of beautiful objects; almost nothing beautiful is not smooth. Ruggedness, sudden projections, or sharp angles are strongly contrary to beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very considerable part of beauty's effect depends on smooth, polished surfaces (smooth leaves, skin, slopes, streams, coats of animals). Even if other constituents are missing, absence of roughness can preserve pleasing effect. Practically: prioritize smoothness of surface and transitions when seeking beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual variation.
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of beautiful bodies vary their direction and form insensibly; they do not persist long in the same straight line but change continuously in a way whose beginning and end are hard to fix. Parts appear 'melted into one another'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the dove, a beautiful bird whose head, neck, body, and tail flow by insensible swells; the neck and breasts of a woman with easy, gradual swellings. For creators: craft forms and descriptions with continuous, subtle variation rather than stark angularity or abrupt changes to enhance beauty.
